x: The construction noise is getting in the way of my studying.
I'm going to graduate from college next year.

ex: 할머니는 언제나 저를 반갑게 맞아 주세요.
x: My grandmother always welcomes me warmly.

ex: 밤에 손톱을 깎으면 안 된다는 것은 미신이에요.
x: The idea that you shouldn't cut your nails at night is a superstition.
t: A famous Korean superstition: writing a living person's name in red ink is bad luck.

x: Sorry I'm late. The traffic was really bad.
e: Literally 'not at ease' + 합니다 — I feel uneasy about what I did.
t: With elders, bosses or customers, 죄송합니다 is safer and more respectful.

x: Yesterday I dropped off my winter coat at the dry cleaner's.
e: Literally 'washing place'; -소 = place for an activity: 세탁소, 주유소.

x: Firefighters risk their lives to save people.
e: Probably 목 'throat' + 숨 'breath' — the breath of life.
t: 목숨을 걸다 'to risk one's life' is the most common collocation.

x: On Children's Day, people give children presents.
e: 어린이 'child' + 날 'day'; it's a public holiday on May 5.

x: I went to see the fireworks on the Han River.
t: Pronounced [불꼰노리]. Seoul's big fireworks festival on the Han River each autumn draws huge crowds.

ex: 진심으로 사과하면 용서를 받을 수 있을 거예요.
x: If you sincerely apologize, you'll probably be forgiven.
t: 용서를 빌다 = to beg for forgiveness; 용서해 주세요 = Please forgive me.

ex: 먼저 이 종이를 반으로 한 번 접으세요.
x: First, fold this paper in half once.
I have a lot of work today, so I'm leaving late.
t: Pronounced [엄무] — nasalization; 업무 sounds formal, while everyday speech just uses 일.

m: to synthesize, to put together, to sum up
x: We'll make a decision after putting together everyone's opinions.
t: Pronounced [종하파다]: ㅂ + ㅎ merge into ㅍ.

ex: 우리 이제 많이 친하니까 반말로 이야기할까요?
x: We're pretty close now, so shall we talk casually?
e: Literally 'half speech' — sentences cut short without the polite ending.
t: Don't switch to 반말 with older people or new acquaintances until they suggest it — it can sound rude.

ex: 어제 주문한 물건이 오늘 택배로 왔어요.
x: The thing I ordered yesterday came by delivery today.
t: 택배 is for packages; food delivery is 배달, as in 배달 음식.

x: I exchanged small gifts with friends on Christmas.
e: From English 'Christmas'; the formal name is 성탄절. In Korea it's more of a couples' holiday.

ex: 우리 반에는 학생이 열다섯 명 있어요.
x: There are fifteen students in our class.
e: Two words: 'class' (우리 반 = our class) and 'half'.
t: 'Half' is common with time: 세 시 반 = 3:30. For 'class' meaning a lesson, use 수업 instead.

x: I feel shy about singing in front of people.
t: 부끄럽다 covers both shyness and shame; 창피하다 is a stronger, 'humiliated' kind of embarrassment.

ex: 서울에서는 대중교통이 편리해서 차가 없어도 돼요.
x: Public transportation in Seoul is so convenient that you don't need a car.
e: Literally 'traffic for the big crowd' — transport for the general public.

x: It was cold, so I slept under a blanket.
e: Slang 이불킥 ('blanket kick') = cringing in bed over an embarrassing memory.
t: 'Cover oneself with a blanket' = 이불을 덮다.

x: The most important thing in life is health.
t: 인생 is life as a whole journey; 생활 is day-to-day living; 생명 is biological life.

x: My face turned red.
e: Being told 얼굴이 작아요 (your face is small) is a compliment in Korea.
t: 얼굴이 좋아 보여요 = You look well (healthy).

ex: 서울의 인구는 천만 명이 조금 안 돼요.
x: Seoul's population is a little under ten million.
e: Literally 'people mouths' — counting the mouths to feed.

forms: casual: 잘 가 · formal: 안녕히 가십시오
x: Thanks for today. Goodbye!
t: Say 가세요 to the person who is leaving. If you leave and they stay, say 안녕히 계세요.

x: I got roses from my boyfriend on my birthday.
e: From an old two-syllable Chinese word for the rose; the syllables aren't reused elsewhere.
t: Count flowers with 송이: 장미 한 송이 'one rose'.

x: Every morning sparrows chirp outside the window.
e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating the chirp of a sparrow or other small bird.
t: Verb: 짹짹거리다 'to chirp'.

forms: 차가 막혀요 · 차가 막혔어요 (casual: 차 막혀)
m: traffic is heavy, to be stuck in traffic
ex: 금요일 저녁에는 차가 막혀서 지하철을 타요.
x: Traffic is bad on Friday evenings, so I take the subway.
e: Literally 'the cars are blocked'; 막히다 is the passive of 막다 'to block'.
t: Pronounced [마키다] — ㄱ followed by ㅎ becomes ㅋ.

ex: 관객들이 앙코르를 외치자 가수가 다시 나왔어요.
x: When the audience shouted for an encore, the singer came back out.
t: 앙코르 공연 can also mean extra shows added because of demand.

ex: 노후를 위해서 매달 조금씩 저축하고 있어요.
x: I'm saving a little every month for my retirement.
t: 노후 준비, 'preparing for retirement,' is a very common phrase.

ex: 피자 한 판을 집으로 배달해 주세요.
x: Please deliver one pizza to my house.
e: Literally 'hand out until it reaches' the customer.
t: To order delivery food, Koreans often say 시켜 먹다: "치킨 시켜 먹을까요?"

ex: 저는 과일을 좋아해요. 예를 들어 사과나 딸기요.
x: I like fruit. For example, apples or strawberries.
e: Literally 'raising an example', from 들다 'to lift, to raise'.

m: to depend on, rely on, lean on
x: I relied on my family a lot when things were hard.
t: Homonym warning: the noun 의지 also means 'willpower', a different word.

x: The weather was nice, so we went for a drive to the beach.
e: From English 'drive', but only for a leisure drive; everyday driving is 운전.
t: Common patterns: 드라이브(를) 가다 'go for a drive' and 드라이브하다.

forms: 제대로 + verb; often 제대로 못 + verb
m: properly, right, as it should be
x: I couldn't sleep properly last night.
e: 제 'its own' + 대로 'according to' — 'in its proper way'.

x: Our company values teamwork above all else.
t: A formal, written word; in conversation people often say 중요하게 생각하다.

x: A big fire broke out at the market yesterday.
t: News says 화재가 발생했다; in conversation people say 불이 났어요.

ex: 축구 경기 후반에 우리 팀이 골을 넣었어요.
x: Our team scored a goal in the second half of the soccer game.
t: Often used with ages: 20대 후반 means 'late twenties'.

m: home, house (honorific); you (to a stranger, distant)
x: Where is your home, sir?
e: From hanja 宅 'house', the respectful word for someone else's home.
t: The plain word is 집; say 댁 for the homes of elders, teachers or customers, but 저희 집 for your own. Used as 'you' (댁은 누구세요?) it sounds distant or even rude.

x: What's your phone number?
t: Phone numbers use Sino-Korean digits; 0 is 공: 010 = 공일공.

ex: 여름이 되면 해수욕장에 사람이 정말 많아요.
x: In summer the beaches get really crowded.
t: Pronounced [해수욕짱]: ㅈ becomes tense after ㄱ. Most officially open only in summer, roughly July to August, when lifeguards are on duty.

x: That claim has no scientific basis.

ex: 이 서류 맨 아래에 서명을 해 주세요.
x: Please sign at the very bottom of this document.
t: In everyday speech people usually say 사인 instead: 여기 사인해 주세요.

forms: casual: 잘 있어 · formal: 안녕히 계십시오
x: Thank you for the meal. Goodbye!
e: 안녕히 (peacefully) + 계세요 (please stay) — 'stay in peace'; said by the one leaving.
t: Used when YOU are leaving and the other person stays, e.g. leaving a shop or someone's home.

m: to shine on, light up; to reflect
ex: 아침 햇살이 창문으로 방 안을 비추고 있어요.
x: The morning sun is shining into the room through the window.
t: 비추다 takes an object (the sun lights up the room); 비치다 doesn't (light shines in).

x: I bought milk in the grocery section of the supermarket.
t: 식품 is food as a product (labels, stores); 음식 is food you cook and eat.

m: to wear, to put on (shoes, socks)
x: I put on sneakers and went out.
e: Related to 신 (shoes), as in 신발. Used for shoes and socks.
t: Pronounced [신따]: the ending tenses after ㄴ in verb stems.

x: My father goes hiking every weekend.
e: Literally 'climbing a mountain' — a hugely popular weekend hobby in Korea.
t: Both 등산을 하다 and 등산을 가다 (go hiking) are common.

ex: 면접 날에 검은색 정장을 입고 갔어요.
x: I wore a black suit on the day of my interview.
t: 정장 is any formal outfit for men or women; 양복 is specifically a men's Western-style suit.

ex: 제 동생은 외향적이라서 친구가 정말 많아요.
x: My younger sibling is outgoing, so they have lots of friends.
The bulgogi is really delicious.

ex: 이 제품은 온라인에서만 판매를 하고 있어요.
x: This product is sold only online.

ex: 요즘은 이혼하는 부부가 점점 늘고 있습니다.
x: These days, more and more couples are getting divorced.
It's a bit far from home to the office.
e: ㄹ drops before ㄴ: 먼 곳 (a far place). Opposite: 가깝다.
t: Common pattern: A에서 B까지 멀어요 = It's far from A to B.

forms: 뵙겠습니다 · 뵙고 · vowel endings use 뵈다: 봬요 · 뵀어요 · 뵐게요
m: to see, to meet (humble, someone senior)
x: Professor, I'll come and see you next week.
e: Humble verb: you lower yourself when meeting someone higher in status. Before vowel endings it switches to 뵈다 (뵈어요 → 봬요).
t: Pronounced [뵙따]: 다 turns tense after ㅂ. The plain words are 보다 and 만나다; use 뵙다 for meeting teachers, bosses or elders, as in 처음 뵙겠습니다 'Nice to meet you'.

x: The government announced a new policy today.
t: Also used for releasing results or albums: 합격자를 발표하다, 신곡을 발표하다.

ex: 제 남자 친구는 요리를 아주 잘해요.
x: My boyfriend is very good at cooking.
t: For a male friend who is not a boyfriend, Koreans say 남사친 or just 친구, since 남자 친구 implies romance.

x: I had internet installed in my new place.
e: Literally 'set up and put in place.'
t: For apps, 앱을 설치하다 is standard; 앱을 깔다 is the casual version.

x: My feet hurt because my shoes are small.

ex: 어젯밤에 모기 때문에 잠을 못 잤어요.
x: I couldn't sleep last night because of mosquitoes.
t: Mosquitoes 'bite' with 물다: 모기한테 물렸어요 'I got bitten by a mosquito.'

x: That actor is very famous in Korea.
t: Don't confuse with the verb 배우다 (to learn): 배워요 means 'I learn', not 'actor'.

forms: 고장 나요 · 고장 났어요 · 고장 날 거예요 · 고장 난 (+noun)
m: to break down, to be out of order
ex: 세탁기가 고장 나서 빨래를 못 해요.
x: The washing machine broke, so I can't do the laundry.
t: Used for machines; for snapped or shattered things, use 부러지다 or 깨지다 instead.

x: I've been so busy that I haven't eaten anything since morning.
t: 아무거나 ('anything is fine') is very common when ordering food or choosing.

x: I lost my wallet, so I went to a nearby police station.
t: Pronounced [경찰써] — 서 becomes tense after the ㄹ.

ex: 뜨거운 국을 급하게 먹어서 혀가 아파요.
x: I ate hot soup too fast, so my tongue hurts.

m: speaking (as a skill or test section)
ex: 말하기 연습을 위해 한국 친구를 만나요.
x: I meet Korean friends to practice speaking.
I go to school on Monday.
t: Pronounced [워료일].

x: Today I made up with the friend I fought with yesterday.
t: Not related to 화 (anger); use N와/과 화해하다 for 'make up with N'.

forms: 번쩍 + 빛나다 / 들다 · 눈을 번쩍 뜨다 · 번쩍이다
m: with a flash; (lift) easily; (eyes) wide open
x: Lightning flashed, and then rain poured down.
e: Manner word (의태어) for a sudden bright flash, extended to anything sudden and easy. Bright-vowel 반짝 is a small, gentle glint.
t: 번쩍 들다 = to lift easily, 눈을 번쩍 뜨다 = eyes snap open, 정신이 번쩍 들다 = to come to one's senses. Verb: 번쩍이다.

ex: 그 영화 감독은 상을 많이 받았어요.
x: That film director has won many awards.
t: In sports, 감독 is the head coach or manager; 코치 is an assistant coach.

x: Using public transportation is more economical.
t: Can mean both 'economic' (경제적 문제) and 'money-saving' (경제적인 차).

ex: 부장님이 회의에서 제 보고서를 많이 칭찬했어요.
x: My manager praised my report a lot in the meeting.
Soldiers must follow their superior's orders.
t: Pronounced [명녕] — ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅇ.

x: It was cold, so I put on a thick sweater.

m: to come up, to come upstairs; to come up to Seoul
x: Take the elevator up to the third floor now.
e: 오르다 (to climb) + 오다 (to come): come up toward the speaker.
t: Koreans say 서울에 올라오다 for traveling to Seoul from anywhere else, no matter the direction on a map.

ex: 밤에 혼자 산에 가는 것은 위험해요.
x: Going to the mountains alone at night is dangerous.

ex: 제 동료는 일을 아주 꼼꼼하게 해요.
x: My coworker does things very meticulously.
e: Doubled 꼼꼼 sounds like careful, step-by-step checking.

ex: 이 문제는 일시적인 현상이니까 걱정하지 마세요.
x: This problem is only temporary, so don't worry.
t: Pronounced [일씨적]: ㅅ after ㄹ is tensed.

x: Boarding for the plane begins 30 minutes before departure.
These two bags are about the same size.
e: 크다 'big' plus the noun suffix -기: literally 'bigness'.
t: 크기 is general size of any object; for clothing sizes, Koreans usually say 사이즈.

ex: 저희 아파트는 반려동물을 키울 수 있어요.
x: Pets are allowed in our apartment building.
t: Pronounced [발려동물]. Now preferred over 애완동물; also 반려견 'companion dog' and 반려묘 'companion cat'.

ex: 다음 주에 중간고사가 있어서 도서관에 가요.
x: I have midterms next week, so I'm going to the library.
t: Often shortened to 중간 in casual talk: 중간 끝났어요?

x: I bought presents for my parents at the airport duty-free shop.

ex: 올해 상반기에 새 제품이 나올 예정입니다.
x: A new product is scheduled to come out in the first half of this year.
e: Literally 'upper half period' — January to June.

x: Actions are much more important than words.

ex: 이 약은 부작용이 거의 없어서 안전해요.
x: This medicine is safe because it has almost no side effects.
t: It's also used figuratively for any unwanted result of a policy or plan.

ex: 내일 회사 면접이 있어서 조금 긴장돼요.
x: I have a job interview tomorrow, so I'm a little nervous.
t: The applicant says 면접을 보다 'take an interview'; the verb 하다 is used less.

x: I added a little salt to the soup.
Rotate your ankles before you exercise.

ex: 동생은 엄마가 언니만 예뻐해서 언니를 질투해요.
x: My little sister is jealous because Mom only dotes on our older sister.
t: 질투 sounds negative and resentful, while 부럽다 is light envy or admiration.

ex: 추석에는 가족이 모여서 조상께 차례를 지내요.
x: On Chuseok, families gather and hold a memorial rite for their ancestors.

ex: 저는 어렸을 때부터 뱀이 정말 무서워요.
x: I've been really scared of snakes since I was little.
Dad, are you coming home early today?
e: Casual word for 아버지 — many adults keep using it too.

x: It was cold, so the child's cheeks turned red.
e: Homonym warning: 볼 is also a form of 보다 'to see,' as in 볼 거예요.
t: 볼 and 뺨 both mean cheek, but slapping uses 뺨: 뺨을 때리다.

m: to fit; to be right, to be correct
ex: 이 바지는 저한테 사이즈가 딱 맞아요.
x: These pants fit me perfectly.
e: Homonym warning: another 맞다 means 'to get hit', as in 비를 맞다 'get rained on'.
t: "맞아요!" means "That's right!" The dictionary form 맞다 is pronounced [맏따].

x: I get a little touchy before exams.
e: Literally 'sharp and quick': nerves or senses that react fast.
t: 예민하다 often means irritable or on edge, not 'sensitive' in the caring sense.

x: That accident was a great misfortune for the family.
t: In fast speech the ㅎ weakens after ㄹ, so it often sounds like [부랭].

forms: 부어요 · 부었어요 · 부을 거예요 · 부은 (+noun) (ㅅ irregular)
ex: 어젯밤에 라면을 먹고 자서 얼굴이 부었어요.
x: I ate ramyeon before bed last night, so my face is puffy.
e: Homonym: 붓다 also means 'to pour,' as in 물을 붓다, conjugated the same way.
t: Swelling is a result, so use the past form for a current state: 발이 부었어요, 'my feet are swollen.'

x: It's raining outside. Do you have an umbrella?
t: 'It's raining' = 비가 와요 or 비가 내려요.

x: I'm in a really good mood today.
t: 기분이 좋아요 = I feel good; 기분이 나빠요 = I'm upset / in a bad mood.

m: to hug, to hold (in one's arms)
ex: 엄마가 우는 아기를 꼭 안아 주었어요.
x: The mom held the crying baby tight.
e: Homonym warning: 안다 is also 알다 'know' with -ㄴ다; 안기다 = be hugged.
t: Pronounced [안따]; don't mix it up with 앉다 'to sit', also pronounced [안따].

m: to interview, to give an interview
ex: 기자가 경기가 끝난 후에 감독을 인터뷰했어요.
x: The reporter interviewed the coach after the game ended.
t: For a job interview, Koreans usually say 면접, not 인터뷰.

m: to leak; to escape (of light, gas, or a secret)
x: It's raining, and water is leaking from the ceiling.
e: Homonym warning: 새다 also means 'to dawn,' as in 밤이 새다.
t: Don't confuse 새다 'to leak' with 세다 'to be strong, to count'; they sound almost the same.

x: The cheering squad sang the fight song loudly.
e: Literally 'respond-and-help group' — a group that backs a team.

x: Your Korean has really improved!
e: Literally 'real power' — what you can actually do.
t: Common collocation: 실력이 늘다 'skills improve'; 실력이 좋다 'to be skilled'.

x: May 5th is Children's Day in Korea, so there's no school.
t: 어린이 is a bit formal, used on signs and holidays; in conversation 아이 or 애 is more common.

x: I have a meeting with someone from a client company this afternoon.
e: Literally 'place you go back and forth with', i.e., trade with.

ex: 판사가 그 사람에게 벌금을 내라고 했어요.
x: The judge ordered that person to pay a fine.
The weather in Seoul is really nice these days.
t: 요즘 and 요새 mean the same; 요새 sounds a little more casual.

x: The kids are playing in the water at the valley stream.
t: Pronounced [물로리]: ㄴ becomes ㄹ after ㄹ. Splashing in a mountain stream is a classic Korean summer family outing.

x: This phone is secondhand, but it's as clean as a new one.
e: 새 'new' plus 것 'thing', written as one word.

x: This fruit is rich in vitamins.

forms: 짱이에요 · 짱이다 · 짱 + adjective (짱 좋아요 = super good)
m: the best, awesome; super, really (before adjectives)
x: The tteokbokki here is seriously the best!
e: Often linked to 장 (長) 'head, chief', said with a tense consonant for emphasis; the origin is not certain.
t: Casual. A thumbs-up with 짱! means 'the best!'. Also found in compounds like 얼짱 'great-looking (literally face-best)'.

x: There is a book on the desk.
e: Opposite of 아래 and 밑. Heads-up: a different 위 means stomach.
t: Korean puts the object first: 책상 위에 = 'desk top-at' → on the desk.

ex: 길이 막히자 차들이 빵빵 경적을 울렸어요.
x: When traffic jammed, the cars started honking.
e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a car horn.
t: Verb: 빵빵거리다 'to honk'. Casual 빵빵하다 means 'full, strong': 에어컨이 빵빵해요 'The AC is blasting'.

ex: 폭설 때문에 비행기 출발이 두 시간 지연됐습니다.
x: Because of the heavy snow, the flight's departure was delayed by two hours.
The water is really cold.
e: For things cold to the touch; cold weather is 춥다. 차가운 사람 = a cold person.

ex: 보고서 마감이 내일이라서 오늘 밤에 써야 해요.
x: The report is due tomorrow, so I have to write it tonight.
t: It also means closing time: 오늘 영업 마감 means 'closed for today'.

x: The river pollution got worse because of the factory.
I stuck the photo in my notebook with glue.
e: Homonym: 풀 also means 'grass'; context makes it clear.

m: to develop, to progress, to advance
ex: 요즘 기술이 아주 빠르게 발전하고 있어요.
x: Technology is advancing very quickly these days.

ex: 그 선수가 이번 경기에서 가장 많은 득점을 했어요.
x: That player scored the most points in this game.
t: Pronounced [득쩜] — ㅈ after ㄱ becomes tense.

forms: casual: 있잖아 · polite: 있잖아요 · 저기, 있잖아요…
m: you know, …; listen, … (bringing up a topic)
x: You know what? I'm getting married next month.
e: 있다 'to exist' + -잖아요 'you know': literally 'there's (this thing), you know'.
t: Pronounced [읻짜나요]. Grabs attention before news or a delicate topic, or reminds: 그 카페 있잖아요, 거기서 만나요.
rel: to be, to exist; to have

x: Our professor researches Korean history.

forms: 으로 after a consonant (손으로) · 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로, 지하철로)
x: I go to school by bus.
e: 으로 after consonants (손으로), 로 after vowels (버스로).
t: Words ending in ㄹ take 로, not 으로: 지하철로, 연필로.

m: to go against, violate; to be out of line; to miss each other
x: That kind of behavior goes against school rules.
t: Pronounced [어근나다] — nasalization; common as 규칙에 어긋나다 'break the rules'.

ex: 아기는 오늘 보건소에서 예방 주사를 맞았어요.
x: The baby got a vaccination at the health center today.
t: Use 맞다 with shots: 주사를 맞다 'to get a shot'.

ex: 남의 말을 너무 신경 쓰지 마세요.
x: Don't worry too much about what others say.
e: Homonym warning: 남 also means 'south' and 'male'; context tells which.

x: I work a part-time job at a café every weekend.
e: From German 'Arbeit' (work), not English; in Korean it means a part-time job.
t: In casual speech it's almost always shortened to 알바, and a part-timer is 알바생.

x: It's really hard to book a campground on weekends.
t: Popular campgrounds open online reservations at a set time and can be fully booked within minutes for summer weekends.

x: My younger sibling doesn't like vegetables.
e: 싫다 (unpleasant) + -어하다. 싫어요! = No, I don't want to!
t: Pronounced [시러하다]: ㅎ in ㅀ is silent before a vowel.

x: The socks are in the bottom drawer.

ex: 저는 주말에 만화를 보는 것을 좋아해요.
x: I like reading comics on the weekend.
e: Literally 'casual pictures'; English 'manhwa' means Korean comics, like 'manga' for Japanese.

forms: subject: 누가 (not 누구가) · object: 누구를 (누굴) · whose: 누구의
x: Who is this person in the photo?
t: With 가, 누구 becomes 누가: 누가 왔어요? (Who came?)

ex: 건강 문제는 전문가와 상담하는 게 좋아요.
x: For health problems, it's best to consult an expert.
e: -가 = professional or expert: 전문가, 작가, 화가.

ex: 무분별한 개발은 자연 파괴로 이어질 수 있습니다.
x: Reckless development can lead to the destruction of nature.
My friend is very kind.
t: 착하다 describes someone's good character; 친절하다 describes kind behavior toward others. Pronounced [차카다].

x: My birthday is May 10th.
t: Say 생일 축하해요! 'Happy birthday!' Use 생신 for elders' birthdays.

x: My older sister got married last year.
t: 'Marry someone' → 사람하고/와 결혼하다 (not 을/를). 'Are you married?' → 결혼했어요?

ex: 배를 타고 한 시간쯤 가면 작은 섬이 있어요.
x: If you take a boat for about an hour, there's a small island.
e: Island names use Sino-Korean -도 instead: 제주도, 독도, 울릉도.

ex: 이 호텔은 위치가 좋아서 지하철역에서 가까워요.
x: This hotel has a good location, so it's close to the subway station.
e: Literally 'the place where something is put'.

forms: 누워요 · 누웠어요 · 누울 거예요 · 누우세요 (ㅂ irregular)
x: I was tired, so I lay down on the bed.
e: Irregular: 누워요; 누워 있다 = to be lying down.

x: My skin was so itchy that I went to the dermatologist.

forms: 너무 + adjective/verb: 너무 비싸요, 너무 좋아요
x: This bag is too expensive.
e: From 넘다 (to go over) — 'too much'; now often just means 'so, really'.
t: Originally negative ('too much'), but now also used positively: 너무 좋아요 = I love it.

ex: 이 신발을 큰 사이즈로 교환하고 싶어요.
x: I'd like to exchange these shoes for a bigger size.
t: Use N을/를 N(으)로 교환하다: "exchange A for B." In casual speech, 바꾸다 is more common.

x: I've decided to work out every day in the new year.
t: The standard greeting is 새해 복 많이 받으세요 — literally 'receive many blessings in the new year'.

x: Complaints from customers kept coming in.
e: Literally 'not even' — things feel unfair or off balance.

forms: 골고루 + verb: 골고루 먹어요, 골고루 나눠요
m: evenly, equally; a little of everything
ex: 건강을 위해서 음식을 골고루 먹어야 해요.
x: For your health, you should eat a balanced variety of food.
e: An emphatic, rhyming form of 고루 'evenly'.
t: 골고루 먹다 is the standard way to say 'eat a balanced diet' — parents say it to picky kids.

ex: 회의에서 한국어 통역을 해 주실 수 있어요?
x: Could you interpret into Korean at the meeting?
t: 통역 is spoken interpreting; 번역 is written translation.

ex: 은행에 갈 때 신분증을 꼭 가져가세요.
x: Be sure to bring your ID when you go to the bank.
e: Literally 'status proof'. -증 = certificate or card: 학생증, 운전면허증.

x: Could you lend me an eraser?
e: From 지우다 'to erase' plus -개 'tool': like 덮개 'cover'.

m: cheer up; hang in there; you can do it
ex: 내일 시험이 있죠? 너무 걱정하지 말고 힘내세요!
x: You have an exam tomorrow, right? Don't worry too much — you've got this!
e: 힘 'strength' plus 내다 'bring out': literally 'bring out your strength'.

x: When the song ended, everyone clapped.
t: Pronounced [박쑤]. Clap is 박수를 치다; hosts say 박수 부탁드립니다 'a round of applause, please'.

ex: 이 떡집은 우리 엄마 단골 가게예요.
x: This rice cake shop is my mom's regular place.
e: Native word. It first meant the shaman a family always called on (단골무당), then a regular customer or shop.
t: 단골 can mean the person (단골손님) or the place (단골집). Regulars often get a little extra for free, called 서비스 or 덤.

x: Thousands of people gathered at the weekend festival.
t: For tens of thousands, Korean uses 수만 ('several 만'), not '수십 천'.

ex: 한국은 고령화가 아주 빠르게 진행되고 있습니다.
x: Korea's population is aging very rapidly.
e: Literally 'becoming high in age.' -화 = '-ization': 현대화, 세계화.
t: Often paired in news as 저출산 고령화, 'low birth rate and aging population.'

forms: 이나 after a consonant (책이나), 나 after a vowel (커피나)
m: or; … or something; as many as
x: Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
t: With numbers it shows surprise: 세 시간이나 기다렸어요 'I waited a whole three hours.'

x: Stress has a direct effect on your health.
t: 직접 alone usually means 'in person, oneself' (직접 만들었어요); 직접적 means 'direct' in a logical sense.

x: It snowed a lot yesterday.
e: Snow is said with a longer vowel.
t: 눈 also means 'eye'. Context tells them apart: 눈이 와요 (it snows) vs 눈이 아파요 (my eyes hurt).

x: You should respect other people's privacy.
t: Common phrase: 사생활 침해 'invasion of privacy', often in news about celebrities.

forms: 이든지 after a consonant (무엇이든지) · 든지 after a vowel (누구든지) · short form: (이)든
x: If you have any questions, ask me anytime.
t: With question words it means 'any-': 누구든지 'anyone', 뭐든지 'anything', 어디든지 'anywhere'. In speech it's often shortened: 뭐든 괜찮아요.

ex: 사고를 방지하기 위해 안전 교육을 합니다.
x: We hold safety training to prevent accidents.

ex: 요즘은 친환경 제품을 사는 사람이 많아요.
x: These days a lot of people buy eco-friendly products.

ex: 밥을 너무 빨리 먹으면 소화가 잘 안 돼요.
x: If you eat too fast, you won't digest well.
e: Literally 'dissolve and transform' — food breaking down.
t: 소화가 안 돼요 is the everyday way to say 'I have indigestion.'

x: I messed up an important exam because of a cold.
e: Probably linked to 망하다 'to go to ruin, go bankrupt'.
t: Everyday collocations: 시험을 망치다 'bomb a test', 분위기를 망치다 'kill the mood'.

ex: 경주에는 신라 시대의 유적이 많이 남아 있어요.
x: Many historic sites from the Silla period remain in Gyeongju.
t: 유적 is a place or site; 유물 is an object you can carry.

m: to continue, go on; to be connected, lead to
x: The meeting went on until late at night.
t: Also 'lead to': 작은 실수가 큰 사고로 이어질 수 있어요 'a small mistake can lead to an accident.'

m: to ignore, to disregard; to look down on
x: Don't ignore what I say.
e: Literally 'not look' — act as if you don't see it.
t: It also means 'to look down on someone': 어리다고 무시하면 안 돼요.

ex: 길을 걷는데 갑자기 비가 내리기 시작했어요.
x: I was walking down the street when it suddenly started raining.
The employees worked according to the boss's instructions.
e: Literally 'point and show' what to do.

m: to break (a rule, promise, law), to violate
ex: 친구가 또 약속을 어겨서 화가 났어요.
x: I got angry because my friend broke a promise again.
t: The opposite is 지키다: 약속을 지키다 'keep a promise' vs. 약속을 어기다 'break a promise.'

ex: 그 사건의 재판은 다음 달에 열립니다.
x: The trial for that case will be held next month.
t: 재판을 받다 means 'to stand trial.'

ex: 오늘 줄무늬 티셔츠를 입고 학교에 갔어요.
x: I wore a striped T-shirt to school today.
t: Pronounced [줄무니] — ㅢ after a consonant sounds like ㅣ.

forms: Use with Sino numbers: 1회, 2회, 3회 (일 회, 이 회, 삼 회)
x: This class meets twice a week.
e: The formal, written counterpart of 번; seen on schedules, labels and TV episodes.
t: In everyday speech say 두 번 'twice'; 2회 sounds formal and appears mostly in writing.

ex: 우리 회사는 매년 건강 검진을 받아요.
x: Everyone at our company gets a health checkup every year.

m: to get hurt, to be injured
x: I hurt my leg while playing soccer.
e: Sounds exactly like 닫히다 (to be closed) — context tells them apart.

ex: 담배를 피우면 암에 걸릴 위험이 높아져요.
x: Smoking raises your risk of getting cancer.
t: Diseases take 걸리다: 암에 걸리다, 감기에 걸리다.

ex: 이번 달 영업 실적이 아주 좋아요.
x: Our sales results this month are very good.
The current temperature in Seoul is 5 degrees below zero.
e: Literally 'appearing and existing' — what is here now.
t: 현재 is more formal than 지금 and is common in news and reports.

ex: 엄마, 학교 다녀왔습니다! 오늘 정말 배고파요.
x: Mom, I'm home from school! I'm really hungry today.
e: Past form of 다녀오다 'go and come back': literally 'I went and came back'.

x: It was so cold my whole body was shaking.
e: Manner word (의태어) for shaking hard. Bright-vowel 달달 is a smaller tremble: 다리를 달달 떨다.
t: 덜덜거리다 is also used for an old machine or car rattling.

m: to get angry (at someone), to lose one's temper
x: My mom got angry because I came home late.
t: 화가 나다 is feeling angry; 화내다 is showing it, usually at someone: 저한테 화내지 마세요.

forms: 최소한 + amount: 최소한 한 시간 · 최소한의 (+noun)
ex: 하루에 최소한 물을 여덟 잔은 마셔야 해요.
x: You should drink at least eight glasses of water a day.

m: to give birth to, to have (a baby); to lay (eggs)
x: My older sister had a beautiful baby girl last month.
e: Native verb. It is the mirror of 태어나다: the mother 낳다 'gives birth', the baby 태어나다 'is born'.
t: Pronounced [나타]: ㅎ and ㄷ merge into ㅌ; before a vowel the ㅎ is silent, so 낳아요 sounds like [나아요]. That makes it sound just like 나아요 from 낫다 'to get better'.

x: Please show your ticket at the museum entrance.
Australia's seasons are the opposite of Korea's, so December is summer.
e: Shortened from an old character spelling of 'Australia' plus 'continent'; the syllables don't help.
t: The English name 오스트레일리아 exists too, but everyday Korean almost always uses 호주.

ex: 겨울 방학에 가족들과 스키를 타러 갔어요.
x: During winter break, I went skiing with my family.
t: Skiing uses 타다 'to ride': 스키를 타다, just like 자전거를 타다.

ex: 요즘은 온라인으로 수업을 듣는 학생이 많아요.
x: These days many students take classes online.
e: From English 'online'; pronounced [올라인] because ㄴ before ㄹ becomes ㄹ.

forms: Same form after any noun, with or without batchim: 꽃처럼, 학생처럼
x: My younger sibling sings as well as a singer.
t: N처럼 and N같이 are interchangeable: 꽃처럼 = 꽃같이 'like a flower'.
rel: to be the same, be like

x: The temperature dropped a lot this morning.
t: 기온 is only for air temperature; for water, rooms or bodies, use 온도.

x: After the graduation ceremony, I took a commemorative photo with my family.
t: Used for any photo marking an occasion or a visit. To ask a passer-by: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?

x: I found a lot of travel information online.

ex: 이 동작은 어려워서 몇 번 더 연습해야 해요.
x: This move is hard, so I need to practice it a few more times.
t: In dance class you'll hear 동작을 크게 하세요 'make your moves bigger'. 동작이 빠르다 / 느리다 = to be quick / slow in moving.

x: The monthly rent for this studio is 500,000 won.
t: Korea also has 전세: you pay one large deposit, get it back later, and pay no monthly rent.

x: In work life, relationships with people are really important.
t: 계 is commonly pronounced [게]: [인간관게].

x: Whoa, it snowed a lot!
e: A stretched form of 와 'wow', with 우 added for extra excitement.
t: Bright and a little childlike, but adults use it too when genuinely impressed.

x: Even so, I like this job.
e: 그렇다 'to be so' + -아도 'even if' — 'even if that's so'.

ex: 그 친구는 SNS 팔로워가 만 명이 넘어요.
x: That friend has over ten thousand followers on social media.
t: 팔로우하다 = to follow; 맞팔 (casual) = following each other.

x: I feel really proud that I finished a difficult task.
e: Originally 'full to bursting': picture your chest swelling with satisfaction.
t: Pronounced [뿌드타다]: the final ㅅ (sounding ㄷ) plus ㅎ becomes ㅌ.

x: I answered the teacher's question in a loud voice.
t: Pronounced [대다파다]. Answer something → ~에 대답하다.

ex: 비가 그친 후에 하늘에 무지개가 떴어요.
x: After the rain stopped, a rainbow appeared in the sky.
e: Probably from old words for 'water' and 'gate' — a water gate in the sky.

ex: 저는 땅콩 알레르기가 있어서 늘 조심해요.
x: I have a peanut allergy, so I'm always careful.
e: 땅 'ground, earth' + 콩 'bean': the bean that grows underground.
t: Peanut butter is 땅콩버터. Roasted peanuts are a common snack served with beer (안주).

m: to manage, to take care of, to maintain
x: I exercise every day to take good care of my health.
t: Pronounced [괄리하다]: ㄴ next to ㄹ becomes ㄹ.

m: going to work, getting to work
ex: 출근 시간에는 지하철에 사람이 정말 많아요.
x: The subway is really crowded during rush hour.

m: topic of conversation, talk of the town
x: That movie is the talk of the internet these days.
t: 화제가 되다 means 'to become a hot topic'; 화제를 바꾸다 means 'to change the subject.'

x: Summer in Korea is very hot.
I bought a used bike to save money.
t: Usually goes before a noun: 중고차, 중고 책, 중고 거래 (secondhand trading).

x: Where is this week's meetup?
e: Literally 'ground and place' — two 'place' syllables together.

x: I made a quick sandwich for breakfast.
e: From English 'sandwich', with extra vowels added: 샌-드-위-치.

ex: 그 사람은 정직해서 거짓말을 하지 않아요.
x: That person is honest, so they don't lie.
t: Pronounced [정지카다]; 정직하다 is morally honest, 솔직하다 is frank about feelings.

ex: 판타지 드라마라서 주인공이 시간 여행을 해요.
x: It's a fantasy drama, so the main character travels through time.
t: Popular mixes include 로맨스 판타지 'romance fantasy', often adapted from web novels and webtoons.

forms: 땀을 흘려요 · 땀을 흘렸어요 · 땀을 흘릴 거예요
ex: 오늘 운동을 열심히 해서 땀을 많이 흘렸어요.
x: I worked out hard today, so I sweated a lot.
e: Literally 'to spill sweat'; 흘리다 also means to spill or shed, as in 눈물을 흘리다.
t: 땀이 나다 just says sweat appears; 땀을 흘리다 suggests sweating a lot, often from hard work.
rel: to sweat, to break a sweat

m: to register, to enroll, to sign up
ex: 다음 달부터 요가 학원에 등록할 거예요.
x: I'm going to sign up for a yoga studio starting next month.
e: Literally 'enter into the record' — put your name on the list.
t: Pronounced [등노카다]: ㄹ after ㅇ turns to ㄴ, and ㄱ+ㅎ becomes ㅋ.

m: to adjust, to control, to regulate (amount or level)
x: Please adjust the air conditioner temperature.
t: 조절 is for amounts or levels like temperature or volume; 조정 is for plans, schedules or positions.

ex: 동물원에 있는 코끼리는 코가 아주 길어요.
x: The elephant at the zoo has a very long trunk.
e: Probably from 코 'nose' + 길다 'long': the long-nosed animal.

forms: 흘러요 · 흘렀어요 · 흐를 거예요 · 흐른 (+noun) (르 irregular)
m: to flow, to run; to pass (time)
x: The Han River flows slowly through the middle of Seoul.
e: Its causative is 흘리다 'to spill, shed'.

x: Drinking a lot of water helps with constipation.

ex: 말이 잘 안 통해서 너무 답답해요.
x: I can't get my point across, so it's really frustrating.
e: Works for a stuffy room and a stuffed-up, frustrated heart — think 'I can't breathe'.
t: Pronounced [답따파다]: the second ㄷ tenses, and ㅂ + ㅎ becomes ㅍ.

ex: 한국 사람들은 설날 아침에 떡국을 먹어요.
x: Koreans eat rice cake soup on Lunar New Year's morning.
e: 떡 'rice cake' + 국 'soup'; eating it on New Year's means you turn a year older.
t: 떡국 몇 그릇 먹었어요? ('How many bowls of 떡국 have you eaten?') is a playful way to ask someone's age.

ex: 매일 새 단어를 열 개씩 외워요.
x: I memorize ten new words every day.
e: Literally 'single word'. 단어를 외우다 = memorize words.

forms: native number + 잔: 커피 한 잔 · 물 두 잔
x: One cup of coffee, please.
e: 커피 한 잔 = a cup of coffee.
t: 한잔하다 means 'to have a drink', usually alcohol: 오늘 한잔해요!

x: Every summer I go to the beach with my family.
I lost my passport, so I have to go to the embassy.
e: Literally 'great-envoy building': where the ambassador (대사) works.

x: Please help me with this.
e: 돕다 (help) + 주다 (give) — helping as a favor.
t: 도와주세요! is the natural way to say 'Help me, please!'

x: Our boss is very kind to the employees.
e: -장 = head of something: 사장, 반장, 교장, 시장.
t: Always add 님 when talking to or about the boss: 사장님. Shop owners are also called 사장님.

x: The autumn sky is really blue.
I'll go back to my hometown during the vacation.
t: 돌아가시다 (honorific) also politely means 'to pass away'.

m: the other person, the other party, counterpart
ex: 대화할 때는 상대방의 말을 잘 들어야 해요.
x: When you talk, you should listen carefully to the other person.

forms: short for 그러면 · reply: 그럼요! (of course!)
m: then, in that case; of course
x: It's raining? Then I'll stay home.
e: Short for 그러면 (if so). 그럼요! = Of course!
t: 그럼 안녕히 계세요 = 'Well then, goodbye.' A natural way to end a conversation.

m: failure (of an exam or selection), rejection
ex: 시험에 불합격해서 내년에 다시 볼 거예요.
x: I failed the exam, so I'll take it again next year.
t: In everyday speech people usually say 시험에 떨어졌어요 instead of 불합격했어요.

m: older sister (of a male); older female friend (of a male)
x: My older sister works at a company.
t: Only males say 누나. Females call an older sister 언니.

m: to be hospitalized, to be admitted to a hospital
ex: 아버지가 교통사고로 일주일 동안 병원에 입원하셨어요.
x: My father was in the hospital for a week after a car accident.
The state must protect the safety of its people.
e: Literally 'country-house': the nation as one family. Homonym 국가 means national anthem.
t: Pronounced [국까]. 국가 is formal; in everyday speech 나라 is more common.

x: I completely agree with that opinion.
t: Use -에 for what you agree with: 그 의견에 동의해요 'I agree with that opinion.'

x: These shoes are really comfortable.
t: 편하게 하세요 = 'Make yourself comfortable.'

m: to open, to be opened; to be held (an event)
x: The window opened by itself because of the wind.
e: Passive of 열다 'to open'; also 'bear fruit': 사과가 열리다.
t: Events are 'opened' in Korean: 축제가 열려요 = the festival is held.

x: I'm moving to a new apartment next month.
e: Both parts mean 'move' — moving house. 이사 가다 = to move away.

x: Seoul has long been the center of Korea's economy.

ex: 이 지역 사람들은 대부분 농업에 종사합니다.
x: Most people in this area work in agriculture.
e: Literally 'farming industry'; -업 = industry: 농업, 산업, 어업.

m: to pass by, to go past; (of time) to go by
x: The bus just went right past the stop.
There are more girls in our class.
The athletes train every morning.
t: Pronounced [훌련] — ㄴ becomes ㄹ next to ㄹ.

ex: 두 회사의 제품은 디자인이 아주 유사해요.
x: The two companies' products are very similar in design.
t: A more formal, written word for 비슷하다; use 비슷하다 in everyday speech.

ex: 다음 주에 떠나는 동료의 송별회를 열었어요.
x: We threw a farewell party for a coworker leaving next week.

m: to develop, to create (products, land, skills)
x: That company developed a new cell phone.

forms: native number + 병: 물 한 병 · 맥주 두 병
x: Two bottles of cola, please.
e: Also the noun 'bottle': 물 한 병 = a bottle of water.
t: Don't confuse with 병 (病) 'illness', as in 병원 'hospital'.

m: to walk (to), to go on foot
x: The weather was nice, so I walked to work today.
e: 걷다 (to walk) + 가다 (to go): literally 'walk and go.'

x: Good quality is our product's competitive edge.
t: Pronounced [경쟁녁] — nasalization.

x: I'll send you a message on KakaoTalk when I get home.
e: Short for 카카오톡 'KakaoTalk'; 톡 is from English 'talk'.
t: Casual. Almost everyone in Korea uses this messenger app, so 카톡 is used like 'text': 카톡해 'text me', 카톡 왔어요 'I got a message'.

ex: 산속에서는 휴대폰 통신이 잘 안 돼요.
x: Cell phone reception is poor in the mountains.
t: 통신사 is your mobile carrier, and 통신비 is your phone bill.

forms: 사람이 · 사람을 · honorific: 분 · plural: 사람들
x: There are so many people in the park.
e: Add it to a country for nationality: 한국 사람 (Korean), 미국 사람 (American).

ex: 겨울에는 공기가 건조해서 피부가 자주 가려워요.
x: In winter the air is dry, so my skin often gets itchy.

ex: 어머니가 끓여 주신 된장찌개가 정말 맛있어요.
x: The doenjang stew my mother made is really delicious.
e: 된 'thick' + 장 'fermented sauce': the thick paste, unlike runny soy sauce.
t: Most often eaten as 된장찌개, one of the most common Korean home dishes.

m: police box, small local police station
ex: 지갑을 주워서 근처 파출소에 갖다 줬어요.
x: I found a wallet and took it to the nearby police box.
e: Literally 'place officers are dispatched from'; -소 = place: 연구소, 주유소.

x: I'm busy these days because I have a lot of work.

ex: 회원 가입을 하면 할인을 받을 수 있어요.
x: If you sign up as a member, you can get a discount.
t: The verb takes 에: 동아리에 가입하다 (join a club), 보험에 가입하다 (get insurance).

x: I went shopping at the department store on the weekend.
e: From English 'shopping' + 하다 (do); 쇼핑몰 = shopping mall.

ex: 저런 가방은 어디에서 살 수 있어요?
x: Where can I buy a bag like that?
e: Short for 저러한, from 저렇다 'to be like that (over there)'.

x: My car was out of gas, so I stopped by a gas station.
t: Koreans say 기름을 넣다, literally 'put in oil', for filling up with gas.

x: I heated the rice in the microwave for two minutes.
e: 전자 'electronic' + English 'range' (a stove) — a Konglish blend, not 'microwave'.

m: a considerable number, a good many
ex: 우리 회사 직원 상당수가 재택근무를 원합니다.
x: A considerable number of our company's employees want to work from home.

ex: 국어 시간에 유명한 시를 한 편 외웠어요.
x: In Korean class, I memorized a famous poem.
e: Homonym warning: 시 also means 'o'clock' and 'city'.
t: Count poems with 편: 시 한 편 'one poem'.

forms: Sino-Korean number + 원: 천 원 · 만 원
x: This milk is 2,000 won.
e: Originally 'round', for round coins — same root as Japanese yen and Chinese yuan.
t: Ask prices with 얼마예요? 10,000원 is 만 원, not 일만 원.

m: to claim, to argue, to insist
x: He kept insisting that he was right.
t: Usually used with -다고: 옳다고 주장하다 'to insist that one is right'.

x: Every morning the rooster crows 'cock-a-doodle-doo'.
e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a rooster's crow.
t: Animal sounds usually take 하고 울다: 꼬끼오 하고 울다 'to crow'. Chicks say 삐약삐약.

x: There are lots of parks in my neighborhood.
e: 동 (village) + native 네. City neighborhoods are named 'X동' in addresses.

x: I exercise every morning.

forms: 돌아요 · 돌았어요 · 돌 거예요 · 도세요 (ㄹ drops)
m: to turn; to go around, to spin
x: Turn left in front of the bank over there.
t: The ㄹ drops before -세요: say 도세요, not 돌으세요.
rel: to go back, to go around

x: I went on the trip after getting my parents' permission.
t: 허락을 받다 'get permission' and 허락을 구하다 'ask permission' are the key collocations.

ex: 우리 아이는 일부터 백까지 숫자를 읽을 수 있어요.
x: Our child can read the numbers from one to a hundred.
e: Literally 'counting letters'; the ㅅ in 숫 is an added linking sound.
t: Pronounced [수짜].

x: If I win the lottery, I'll become rich.
t: Korean has no common adjective for 'rich' — say 부자예요 or 돈이 많아요.

x: The children observed the ants closely.
In the evening, the sun sets in the west.
I tiptoed so the baby wouldn't wake up.
e: Manner word (의태어) for moving quietly so no one notices. Dark-vowel 슬금슬금 is the standard pair, with a more furtive, sly feel.
t: Typically with movement verbs: 살금살금 다가가다 'to creep up on'.

ex: 여행을 가려고 돈을 열심히 저축하고 있어요.
x: I'm working hard to save money for a trip.
t: Pronounced [저추카다] — ㄱ + ㅎ become an aspirated ㅋ.

ex: 요즘 서울 집값이 너무 올라서 걱정이에요.
x: I'm worried because house prices in Seoul have gone up so much lately.
t: Pronounced [집깝]: ㄱ becomes tense after ㅂ. News headlines often say 집값이 폭등하다 'house prices soar'.

x: I played ping-pong with coworkers during lunch.
t: Pronounced [탁꾸] — ㄱ after ㄱ becomes tense.

x: I pack gimbap when I go on a picnic.
e: 김 (dried seaweed) + 밥 (rice). Not the surname 김 — just a look-alike.
t: Both [김밥] and [김빱] are accepted pronunciations.

ex: 회사 규정에 따라 사무실에서는 담배를 피울 수 없어요.
x: Under company rules, you can't smoke in the office.
e: Literally 'a rule that has been fixed.'

ex: 아침에 안개가 많이 껴서 앞이 잘 안 보여요.
x: There's so much fog this morning that I can't see ahead well.

ex: 그 운동선수는 매일 여섯 시간씩 연습해요.
x: That athlete practices six hours every day.
e: 선수 is literally 'chosen hand': someone picked for their skill.

ex: 자기 생각만 하는 것은 너무 이기적이에요.
x: Thinking only about yourself is too selfish.
t: Used like an adjective: 이기적이다, or 이기적인 + noun (이기적인 사람 = a selfish person).

ex: 우리 집에는 침실이 두 개 있어요.
x: Our home has two bedrooms.
e: Literally 'sleeping room'. -실 = room: 욕실, 교실, 사무실.

ex: 길이 막혀서 간신히 비행기 시간에 맞췄어요.
x: The roads were jammed, so I barely made my flight.

ex: 다음 주에 과 친구들이랑 엠티 가요.
x: Next week I'm going on an MT with friends from my department.
e: Konglish: from the initials of English 'membership training', also written MT.
t: Usually an overnight trip to a rented country guesthouse with games, cooking and drinking, especially common for freshmen in the spring semester.

x: Many citizens gathered in the square on the weekend.
t: 시민 is a city's residents or citizens in a civic sense; 국민 is the people of a whole nation.

x: Sunscreen protects your skin from sunlight.
t: Pattern: A로부터 B를 보호하다 = protect B from A.

x: The toilet was clogged, so I called a repairman.
The broken part needs to be replaced.

ex: 환경 오염은 바다 생태계를 위협하고 있습니다.
x: Environmental pollution is threatening the ocean ecosystem.
I exercise every day for my health.
t: 건강하세요! ('Stay healthy!') is a common warm goodbye or New Year wish.

x: Please go to the right.
t: Use 으로 for direction: 오른쪽으로 도세요 = turn right. Synonym: 오른편.

x: I run in the park every morning.
t: Pronounced [달리다]. In everyday speech 뛰다 is very common for 'run'.

forms: 늘어요 · 늘었어요 · 늘 거예요 · 는 (+noun) (ㄹ drops)
m: to increase, to grow; to improve (skills)
x: I practiced every day, so my cooking skills improved.
e: Causative 늘리다 'to increase something' comes from it.

x: My wallet and phone are inside my bag.
e: Also means gut or heart: 속이 안 좋아요 'my stomach is upset'.
t: 안 is the general 'inside'; 속 suggests deep inside something filled, like a bag, forest or water.

x: If you grow plants in your room, the air gets better.
e: Literally 'planted thing'; its partner is 동물, 'moving thing.'
t: Pronounced [싱물] — nasalization of ㄱ before ㅁ.

forms: 틀어요 · 틀었어요 · 틀 거예요 · 트세요 (ㄹ drops)
m: to turn on (TV, radio, AC, music); to twist, to turn
x: It was so hot that I turned on the air conditioner.
e: Core idea 'twist': old dials and faucets were twisted on.
t: 틀다 is common for media and AC; for lights use 켜다.

x: I ordered a hamburger and a cola.
e: From English 'cola'. Ask for 콜라 rather than 'Coke'.

ex: 그는 자신이 범인이 아니라는 것을 증명했어요.
x: He proved that he wasn't the culprit.
t: 증명서 means certificate, as in 재학 증명서 (proof of enrollment).

x: He worked up the courage and confessed his feelings to her.
t: In dating culture, 고백 is asking someone to be your boyfriend or girlfriend.

ex: 우리는 서울에서 이틀 동안 시내 관광을 했어요.
x: We went sightseeing around Seoul for two days.
e: Literally 'viewing the light' — taking in the sights.

x: During summer break, I swam at the beach.
e: 바다 'sea' + 가 'edge', linked by ㅅ; compare 강가 'riverside', 길가 'roadside'.
t: Pronounced [바다까] — the ㅅ just makes the ㄱ tense.

forms: 주가 · 주를 · 이번 주 · 다음 주 · 지난주
x: I'm going on a trip next week.
e: 이번 주 = this week, 다음 주 = next week, 지난주 = last week.
t: For a duration use 일주일 (one week) or 이 주 (two weeks).

x: When the water boils, turn the heat down.
e: Add -이- to get 끓이다 'to boil something'.
t: Pronounced [끌타]; 끓어요 sounds like [끄러요].

m: to take (something) along, to take away
x: It's raining. Take an umbrella with you.
e: 가지다 (hold) + 가다 (go) — carry it away; compare 가져오다 (bring).
t: Takes things away from where you are; for people use 데려가다.

x: I'll return the book I borrowed last time today.
t: Usually used with 에 as a time word: 지난번에 'last time'.

ex: 키가 작아서 손이 선반에 안 닿아요.
x: I'm short, so my hand doesn't reach the shelf.
t: Pronounced [다타], and the ㅎ goes silent before vowels: 닿아요 [다아요].

m: ancestral rite, memorial service for ancestors
x: My family holds an ancestral rite every major holiday.
e: Literally 'offering and worship': food is set out for ancestors' spirits.
t: The verb used is 지내다: 제사를 지내다 (to hold an ancestral rite).

x: The interviewer asked me about my experience.
Thank you for showing me the way.
e: From 고맙다 (to be grateful) — the native Korean partner of 감사합니다; both are polite.

x: These pants are too short for me.
e: Opposite of 길다; 짧은 머리 = short hair.
t: Pronounced [짤따]; 짧아요 [짤바요]. For a short person, say 키가 작다, not 짧다.

x: I feel refreshed after taking a walk in the morning.
On weekends, I relax and enjoy movies at home.
e: Related to 즐겁다 'to be fun, joyful'.
t: 즐겨 + verb means 'often, by preference': 즐겨 듣는 음악 'music I like to listen to.'

x: After class, I always review at home.
t: Pronounced [복쓰파다]; pairs with 예습하다 'preview before class'.

m: to be produced, to be manufactured
x: This car is produced in Korea.

m: to send, to mail (a letter, package); to fry (pancakes)
ex: 어제 우체국에 가서 고향에 소포를 부쳤어요.
x: Yesterday I went to the post office and mailed a package home.
e: Homonym: 전을 부치다 means 'to pan-fry Korean pancakes'.
t: Don't confuse with 붙이다 'to stick, attach' — same pronunciation [부치다].

x: I'm a university student. I study Korean.
t: Pronounced [대학쌩]: ㅅ after a ㄱ batchim becomes tense ㅆ.

ex: 우리의 첫 만남은 학교 앞 작은 도서관에서였어요.
x: Our first meeting was at a small library in front of the school.
e: From 만나다 'to meet' plus the noun ending -ㅁ.

ex: 저기 다음 사거리에서 오른쪽으로 돌아 주세요.
x: Please turn right at the next intersection up there.
e: 사 'four' plus native 거리 'street': where four streets meet.
t: Common in directions: 사거리에서 왼쪽으로 가세요 "Go left at the intersection."

x: Our teacher is very kind.
e: Literally 'born before' + 님 (honorific) — someone who is ahead of you.
t: Also a respectful title for doctors and other professionals. Use honorific verbs: 선생님이 오세요.

m: besides, on top of that, moreover
ex: 게다가 그 식당은 가격도 아주 싸요.
x: On top of that, the restaurant is very cheap too.
e: Probably a contraction of 거기에다가 'adding to that'.

m: to oppose, to be against, to object
x: At first, my parents were against my marriage.
t: The noun 반대 also means 'opposite': 반대 방향 = the opposite direction.

ex: 여름에는 달고 맛있는 복숭아가 많이 나와요.
x: In summer, lots of sweet, delicious peaches come into season.
e: Peach blossoms are 복숭아꽃, or in poetic style 복사꽃.
t: Pronounced [복쑹아] — tensing after ㄱ.

x: I talked with my friend for a long time.
t: In speech it's often shortened to 얘기: 얘기해요.

ex: 이 문제에 대해 여러분의 의견을 말해 주세요.
x: Please share your opinions on this issue.

ex: 언니는 성격이 차분해서 화를 잘 안 내요.
x: My older sister has a calm personality, so she rarely gets angry.
e: Describes a quiet, settled nature; also used for calm colors or atmosphere.
t: 차분하다 is a calm personality or mood; 침착하다 is staying cool in a crisis.

ex: 감기 증상이 있으면 집에서 푹 쉬세요.
x: If you have cold symptoms, get plenty of rest at home.
t: Doctors often ask 어떤 증상이 있으세요? — 'What symptoms do you have?'

ex: 두 사람은 정말 잘 어울리는 커플이에요.
x: They really are a perfect couple.
e: From English 'couple'; Konglish spin-offs include 커플룩 'matching outfits' and 커플링 'couple rings'.

ex: 어릴 때 제 꿈은 과학자가 되는 거였어요.
x: When I was little, my dream was to become a scientist.
e: -자 = person who does it: 과학자, 기술자, 담당자.

x: What's the reason you were late?
e: Literally 'reason + cause' — 왜? (why?) is answered with an 이유.

ex: 이삿짐을 다 옮기는 데 하루가 걸렸어요.
x: It took a whole day to move all our stuff.
e: 이사 'moving' + 짐 'load, luggage,' joined by an extra ㅅ.
t: Pronounced [이사찜] or [이삳찜] — the added ㅅ makes 짐 tense.

forms: 써요 · 썼어요 · 쓸 거예요 · 쓰세요 (ㅡ drops)
m: to wear, to put on (hat, glasses, mask); to hold up (umbrella)
x: It was raining outside, so I used an umbrella.
e: For the head and face: 모자/안경/마스크를 쓰다; 우산을 쓰다 = hold an umbrella.
t: Korean has different 'wear' verbs: 입다 clothes, 신다 shoes/socks, 쓰다 hats/glasses/masks.

x: That actor got divorced after two years of marriage.
e: Literally 'leave the marriage'; the opposite of 결혼.

ex: 회원이 되면 책을 무료로 빌릴 수 있어요.
x: If you become a member, you can borrow books for free.

ex: 이 박물관은 입장료가 하루 종일 무료예요.
x: Admission to this museum is free all day.
t: 무료 is the neutral word on signs and menus; 공짜 is the casual spoken word.

x: The sunlight was strong, so I put on sunglasses.
e: From English 'sunglasses'; count it as one item: 선글라스 하나.
t: Glasses and sunglasses take the verb 쓰다, not 입다: 선글라스를 쓰다.

m: to erase, to delete; to remove (makeup, stains)
x: I deleted the photos I didn't need from my phone.
e: Related to 지우개 'eraser': -개 turns the verb into a tool.

ex: 항상 저를 도와주셔서 선생님께 정말 감사하다고 말씀드렸어요.
x: I told my teacher I was really grateful to her for always helping me.
t: 감사합니다 and 고맙습니다 mean the same; 감사합니다 sounds slightly more formal and is safest with strangers.

ex: 이 필터를 쓰면 피부가 더 좋아 보여요.
x: If you use this filter, your skin looks better.
t: Korean camera apps are known for beauty filters. #노필터 'no filter' tags an unedited photo.

x: The mosquito bite is really itchy.
t: 가렵다 is itchy; 간지럽다 is ticklish, though people also use it casually for itchy.

m: to admit, to acknowledge; to recognize (as valid)
x: He honestly admitted his mistake.
e: Literally 'recognize and settle' — accept something as fact.

x: After entering college, I joined a photography club.
e: Native word meaning 'a group of like-minded people'; the standard word for campus clubs.
t: 동아리 is used for school and college clubs; adult hobby groups are usually 동호회.

x: In the countryside you can see the stars well at night.
e: 별 다섯 개 = five stars (a rating). Unrelated to 별로 (not really).

m: writing (as a skill or test section)
x: I ran out of time on the writing test.

forms: Sino-Korean · dates, money, minutes, phone numbers, floors (이 층, 이월)
x: My room is on the second floor.
e: Homonyms: 이 also means 'this' and 'tooth' — context tells you which.
t: Don't mix it up with 이 'this' or the subject particle 이 — context makes it clear.

ex: 어제 친구랑 재미있는 얘기를 많이 했어요.
x: Yesterday I talked about a lot of fun stuff with a friend.
t: 얘기 is casual and spoken; 이야기 is preferred in writing.

forms: 전화를 걸어요 · 걸었어요 · 걸 거예요 · 거세요 (ㄹ drops)
m: to make a phone call, to call
ex: 어제 저녁에 고향에 계신 어머니께 전화를 걸었어요.
x: Yesterday evening I called my mother back home.
e: 걸다 means 'to hang, to hook': you hook up a line to someone.
t: In speech 전화하다 is more common; 전화를 걸다 stresses dialing the call.

m: to boast, to show off, to brag about
ex: 친구가 저에게 새로 산 휴대폰을 자랑했어요.
x: My friend showed off his new phone to me.
e: 자랑 'something to be proud of' + 하다; also gives 자랑스럽다 'proud'.

ex: 이 그래프를 분석하면 변화를 쉽게 알 수 있어요.
x: If you analyze this graph, you can easily see the changes.
e: Literally 'divide and split apart', plus 하다 'to do'.
t: Pronounced [분서카다]: ㄱ plus ㅎ becomes ㅋ.

ex: 퇴근 후에 친구하고 저녁을 먹기로 했어요.
x: I decided to have dinner with a friend after work.
t: 퇴근 후에 'after work' is a very common phrase for evening plans.

x: It was hot, so I bought a cold drink at the convenience store.
t: Pronounced [음뇨수] — ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅁ.

x: My mom makes kimchi with napa cabbage.
e: Probably from an old borrowed reading of Chinese 'white vegetable'; now felt as native.
t: A whole head of cabbage is counted with 포기: 배추 한 포기.

x: Taking photos is prohibited inside the museum.
t: Signs often use it as a suffix: 주차 금지 (no parking), 출입 금지 (no entry).

forms: 세상에! · stronger: 세상에나! · 세상에, 이럴 수가!
m: oh my God!, good heavens!, my goodness
ex: 세상에, 이 많은 음식을 혼자 다 만들었어요?
x: Good heavens, you made all this food by yourself?
e: 세상 'the world' (literally 'upon the world') + 에 'in' — as if saying 'in all the world, how can this be?'
t: Shows amazement or shock, good or bad. 세상에나 is stronger and sounds a bit older or more motherly.

ex: 우리 할아버지는 매일 아침 신문을 읽으세요.
x: My grandfather reads the newspaper every morning.
I always eat breakfast.
e: Both parts mean 'constant' — doubled up for 'always'.

x: Yesterday I paid a fine for running a red light.
t: Common in traffic: 신호 위반 'running a light,' 속도 위반 'speeding,' 주차 위반 'parking violation.'

ex: 여행 중에 친구에게 예쁜 엽서를 보냈어요.
x: I sent my friend a pretty postcard while traveling.
e: Literally 'leaf writing', a message on a single thin sheet.
t: Pronounced [엽써]: the ㅅ becomes tense after the ㅂ batchim.

x: I signed the contract for a new house yesterday.
t: Common patterns: 계약을 하다 'make a contract', 계약이 끝나다 'a contract ends'.

forms: noun + 의 + noun (친구의 책) · 나의 → 내, 저의 → 제, 너의 → 네
x: This is my friend's bag.
e: 나의 shortens to 내 (my), 저의 to 제.
t: As a particle it's usually pronounced [에]. It's often dropped in speech: 친구 책.

x: This café has a quiet, nice atmosphere.
t: Useful phrases: 분위기 있다 'to be atmospheric' and 분위기를 깨다 'to kill the mood'.

forms: 늦게 + verb: 늦게 자요, 늦게 와요
x: I went to bed late last night.
e: 늦다 (to be late) + -게 (adverb ending). Opposite: 일찍 (early).
t: Pronounced [늗께].

x: The government announced that it will expand welfare for the elderly.
That café's interior is really unusual.
Don't drink coffee at night.
e: 밤 'chestnut' is said with a longer vowel.
t: Homonym: 밤 also means 'chestnut'.

m: gasp!, yikes, oh no (sudden surprise or shock)
x: Yikes, I left my wallet at home!
e: A sound word imitating a sharp intake of breath. Doubled, 헉헉 imitates panting.
t: Casual and very common in texts. 헉 is a quick startled reaction; 헐 is more stunned disbelief.

ex: 그는 사랑이 많은 따뜻한 가정에서 자랐어요.
x: He grew up in a warm, loving home.
t: Homonym: 가정 also means 'assumption' (假定); in family contexts it means home.

x: The average score on this test is 75 points.

forms: native number + 권: 책 세 권
x: I borrowed two books from the library.
e: Originally 'scroll'; 책 두 권 = two books.

forms: 인기 있어요 · 인기 있었어요 · 인기 있는 (+noun)
ex: 요즘 젊은 사람들에게 가장 인기 있는 음식이 뭐예요?
x: What food is the most popular with young people these days?
e: Literally 'has people's energy': people are drawn to it.
t: Pronounced [인끼 읻따]: the ㄱ in 인기 is tensed. Opposite: 인기 없다.

forms: time + 부터 (아홉 시부터) · often 부터 … 까지
x: Class starts at nine.
e: Probably from 붙다 (to stick). Pairs with 까지: 9시부터 5시까지 = from 9 to 5.
t: 부터 is mainly for time; for places use 에서: 서울에서 부산까지.

ex: 처음에는 누구나 실수를 할 수 있어요.
x: Anyone can make mistakes at first.
e: Literally 'lose hold with the hand' — a slip of the hand.
t: Pronounced [실쑤] — tensing.

m: to disappear, to be gone, to be lost
x: The wallet I left on the desk is gone.
Korea exports a lot of cars every year.
Please don't talk loudly on the phone in public places.

ex: 빨간 신호일 때는 꼭 멈춰야 해요.
x: You must stop when the light is red.
t: 신호등 is the traffic light itself; 신호 is the signal it shows: 신호가 바뀌었어요.

x: I save half of my salary every month.
Young people's indifference to politics is a problem.
e: 무 'without' + 관심 'interest'. 무- = 'no, without': 무료, 무책임.

x: Please answer the teacher's question clearly.

forms: 직접 + verb: 직접 만들다, 직접 가다
x: I made this cake myself.
e: Literally 'direct contact' — no one in between.
t: Pronounced [직쩝] — the ㅈ tenses after the ㄱ batchim.

ex: 계획을 세우는 것보다 실천하는 것이 더 중요해요.
x: Putting a plan into action is more important than making it.
t: Common pair: 이론과 실천 'theory and practice'.

m: to expand, to enlarge; to zoom in
ex: 글씨가 너무 작아서 사진을 확대해서 봤어요.
x: The writing was too small, so I zoomed in on the photo.
In summer I usually wear T-shirts.
e: From English 'T-shirt', often shortened to 티. 반팔 티 = short-sleeve tee.

ex: 이 영화는 청소년이 볼 수 없습니다.
x: Teenagers are not allowed to see this movie.
e: Literally 'green, young years' — youth in its fresh stage.

m: to talk on the phone, to speak by phone
ex: 어제 친구와 한 시간 동안 통화했어요.
x: I talked on the phone with my friend for an hour yesterday.
t: Use N하고/N와 통화하다 'talk on the phone with N'.

x: This is my favorite place.
e: Also works as a counter: 한 곳, 두 곳.
t: Pronounced [곧]; 곳이 sounds like [고시].

x: My older sister is tall and slim.

m: to work, to be on duty, to serve
ex: 제 형은 은행에서 오 년 동안 근무했어요.
x: My older brother worked at a bank for five years.
e: Literally 'diligent tasks': working at a job.
t: More formal than 일하다; common on job ads and forms: 근무 시간, 근무 장소.

x: This bag is too expensive.
e: Spelled with ㅄ. 밥값 = meal cost.
t: Pronounced [갑]; before a vowel the ㅅ returns as ㅆ: 값이 [갑씨], 값을 [갑쓸].

ex: 우리 집은 학교와 회사 중간에 있어요.
x: My house is halfway between the school and my office.
t: 중간고사 is a midterm exam, and 기말고사 is a final exam.

m: to be burdensome, to feel pressured, to feel like too much
x: An expensive gift feels like a bit much.
e: 부담 'burden' plus -스럽다 'feeling like': it feels like a burden.
t: Koreans also use it for too much attention or kindness, like a stare or a pushy friend.

ex: 다른 사람의 의견을 존중하는 것이 중요해요.
x: It's important to respect other people's opinions.
t: 존중하다 is respecting rights or opinions; 존경하다 is admiring someone, like a teacher or parent.

ex: 밤에 배가 너무 아파서 응급실에 갔어요.
x: My stomach hurt so much at night that I went to the ER.
e: Literally 'room for responding to urgent cases.'
t: Pronounced [응급씰] — the ㅅ after ㄱ becomes tense.

x: How does this food taste?
e: 맛있다 = delicious ('taste exists'); 맛없다 = not tasty.
t: 맛이 is pronounced [마시]. 맛있다 is [마싣따] (also accepted: [마딛따]).

ex: 상황에 적절한 말을 하는 것이 중요해요.
x: It's important to say what fits the situation.
t: 적절하다 means exactly appropriate; 적당하다 leans toward 'moderate, about right'.

x: This job requires specialized knowledge.
e: Literally 'devoted to one gate' — focused on a single field.

ex: 배터리가 얼마 안 남아서 충전해야 해요.
x: My battery is almost dead, so I need to charge it.
t: Say 배터리가 없어요 or 배터리가 다 됐어요 when your phone is dead.

m: to be ugly, to be unattractive
x: Our puppy is ugly, but so cute.
e: 못 'poorly' + 생기다 'to be formed' — the opposite of 잘생기다.

m: to wear (a watch, belt); to kick
x: My father always wears a wristwatch.
e: Homonyms: other 차다 verbs mean 'to be full'; the adjective 차다 means 'cold'.
t: Use 차다 for things worn at the wrist or waist: 시계를 차다, 벨트를 차다.

x: August 15th is the day that celebrates Korea's independence.
t: Pronounced [동닙] — nasalization of both consonants.

m: to get wet, to be wet
x: I didn't have an umbrella, so my clothes got completely wet.
e: Opposite pair: 젖다 (get wet) and 마르다 (get dry).
t: Usually used in the past tense for a current state: 옷이 젖었어요 = my clothes are wet.
